newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS-Gold price steady as Dutch sell bullion.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Gold price steady as Dutch sell bullion.

text.p: The Dutch central bank said on Monday it sold 300 tonnes of gold from its reserves last year, one-fifth of its total holdings, raising $3.8 billion which it will hold as interest-bearing foreign currency reserves.
The amount, some 10 million ounces, is equivalent to around two-thirds of the entire annual output of South Africa, the world's largest gold miner.
But the gold price showed little reaction to the news, fixing in London on Monday afternoon unchanged from its morning setting at $359.60 per ounce.
The announcement confirmed the suspicions of many in the bullion market of a major official sale in the course of 1996.
In Basle Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said central banks of the Group of 10 countries had "no intention" for the time being of selling any gold.
He said other countries were unlikely to follow suit in a bid to plug fiscal deficits and qualify this year as founding members of Europe's single currency in 1999.

"For the time being, there is no intention for (G10) central banks to sell gold," Tietmeyer said, adding there was no "formal agreement" on gold sales but that those attending the meeting had indicated they had no such intentions.
Rumours of central bank selling have been a principal factor behind a dramatic slide in the world bullion price this year.

Gold plunged to a fix of $354.00 an ounce on January 9, its lowest level since October 1993, and a fall of 3-1/4 percent since the start of the year, reflecting ebbing market confidence amid the speculation.
But analysts said even if confirmation of the sale helped the price in the near-term, the news was a blow for the market.
"The news is probably bullish short-term and bearish long-term," said bullion market analyst Andy Smith of Union Bank of Switzerland in London.
He said there may be some initial relief from the fact that the market had absorbed such a large quantity of gold.
"But in the longer term, it's yet another central bank selling gold," he added.
The bank said it had made successive sales during the year but did not specify any dates. Large official sales of metal are usually staggered to limit market impact.

But international price weakness caused rumours to surface. A report from authoritative research group Gold Fields Mineral Services (GFMS) in January also pinpointed accelerating official sales in the second half of 1996. It estimated 123 tonnes had been sold during the period and 208 tonnes in the whole year.
When the gold price plunged in December last year on inreasing speculation, the Dutch central bank denied it had sold any of its bullion reserves when asked by Reuters.
In a statement released on Monday the bank said it had informed the finance ministry of its intention to sell as far back as February last year.

Tony Warwick-Ching, a London-based metals markets analyst at CRU International said it was "disspiriting" that the Netherlands had turned out to be the seller as it was not viewed as an economy which needed the assets.
"It does not have a high national debt or a high budget deficit. That is enough to make you a little uneasy," he said.

The sale leaves the Dutch central bank still holding 1,052 tonnes of bullion, and according to London analysts cuts the proportion of gold and foreign currency reserves held in gold to 22.5 percent, against a world average of 22 percent.
The Dutch bank said proceeds from its sale would be added entirely to foreign exchange reserves and that the transactions would be settled in February and March this year.
A central bank spokesman said the 6.4 billion guilders ($3.60 billion) raised by the sale would be invested in dollar instruments, and possibly other currencies such as marks and yen.
The conversion will lead to a structural improvement in the bank's profits.
Holding foreign exchange instead of gold will lead to an annual increase of 250 million guilders in the profits which the bank transfers to the government.
The latest sale is the country's second major gold divestment since it sold 400 tonnes in 1992.
That news came on the heels of a 200-tonne Belgian sale in the same year and both divestments were a major factor behind gold tumbling to a seven-year low in March 1992 at $326.10.
Belgium subsequently sold 175 tonnes in 1995 and a further 203 tonnes during the first quarter of 1996. It made its first major gold sale in 1989 when it disposed of 127 tonnes.
($1=1.779 Guilder)
